finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so there is nothing to call too wide or too narrow; this file is a first build. The site's existing belt page covers the belt alone and mentions about $175-$500 for belt plus tensioner. Built totals for the tensioner alone, belt reused (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Mazda3 2.0L about $164-$380 (0.4-1.0 hr); midsize 2018 Mazda CX-5 2.5L about $152-$384 (0.3-1.0 hr); truck 2020 Ram 1500 3.6L eTorque about $260-$439 (0.6-1.0 hr); luxury 2008 Lexus LX 570 about $142-$271 (0.5-1.0 hr). So about $150-$440 covers the four examples. That sits around the benchmarks: RepairPal's national average is $338-$413, FIXD gives $235-$267, and YourMechanic's Mazda3 examples run $331-$534. The low ends pair an online parts price with a warranty time of 18 to 36 minutes, which is less than most shops bill for any visit, so about $200 is a more realistic floor at a shop. How solid the labor times are: every low end is a manufacturer-stated time for the example vehicle itself (Mazda 0.4 hr for the 2014-2021 Mazda3 and 0.3 hr for the 2017-2020 CX-5, FCA 0.6 hr for the 2020 Ram 1500 3.6L eTorque including the inspection, Lexus 0.5 hr for the 2008 LX 570). All are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill. The Mazda bulletin prints times against labor codes without a description for each, so it is read, not stated, that the time is for inspecting and replacing the tensioner. Every high end is one general statement that the job takes a mechanic 15 minutes to an hour; Mazda's own 1.0 hr for the turbo CX-30 supports one hour as a top figure, and no source found gives more. Engines where the tensioner is buried (some transverse V6s) can take longer than anything here; none was checked. Parts cautions: aftermarket prices were found only for the two Mazdas (Gates 39390, $115.54 at one seller and $144.80 at another); the Ram and Lexus low ends are the genuine part at an online discount. The Ram example is unusual: its tensioner is a hydraulic unit for the mild-hybrid belt and lists at $279, while the 5.7L V8 Ram tensioner lists at $192 and the older non-hybrid 3.6L one at $511, so truck parts vary widely by engine. The Lexus LX 570 tensioner is cheap for a luxury vehicle ($111 list); the tensioner number Lexus uses on its 4.6L and 5.0L cars lists at $279.43, which would put a luxury total nearer $270-$440. The two Mazda list prices for the same part differ slightly ($220.44 and $223.76), and the Lexus bulletin was read from a copy hosted on a car-review site, not from the NHTSA site. This is an estimate, not a quote and not a diagnosis. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the Mazda bulletin's 0.3 and 0.4 hr are printed against labor codes with no description, for an inspection that replaces the tensioner only if it fails, so they are cross-checks; the Mazda3 and CX-5 lows now use Lexus's 0.5 hr 'R&R' time (not the example vehicles). Built totals at $120-$160/hr: Mazda3 about $176-$380, CX-5 $176-$384. Confidence is low: only two of eight labor figures are for the example vehicle.
extras: A quote often adds a new serpentine belt, since the belt has to come off anyway (a belt alone is roughly $35-$90 in parts on common cars), and one or more idler pulleys. Also possible: new tensioner mounting bolts or a seal where the maker says not to reuse them, a diagnosis fee for a squeal, chirp or rattle, shop supplies and sales tax. A tensioner damaged by a seized alternator, water pump or A/C compressor pulley means that part is quoted separately, and a belt soaked by an oil or coolant leak means the leak is a separate repair. Some engines have a second belt with its own tensioner.
